job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven in the student house on Alder Row, make toast and walk twenty minutes to the Dunmere University engineering block. I'm doing a master's in structural engineering after my civil engineering degree. Mornings are lectures on steel connections, afternoons are the library or the lab, and I do three evening shifts a week stacking shelves at the supermarket. I have about 31,000 in student debt and nothing saved, so a free weekend is rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means my degree keeps its value and the sums I'm learning are still the sums people need. I'd probably post in the student union group that the hype was just companies selling software. Honestly I'd just feel vindicated, because I've never trusted those chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still doesn't fix my problem. The debt is there and there are very few structural jobs near Dunmere, maybe three firms that take graduates. So nothing changes for me except that I can stop worrying about being replaced and go back to worrying about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the supermarket shifts and apply to every consultancy within two hours by train, about 30 applications by next summer. I'd keep doing my calculations by hand first and then check them in the software, like my tutor Mr Okafor taught us. I wouldn't change how I work at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machines, but a bit tight in the chest about money. It's a relief and a worry at once, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the shelf-stacking. Which cost does it really cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays my rent share, which is 340 a month, and that's the whole of it. Books and the train fare to interviews come out of the same wage, so every interview costs me a shift. The one thing I'd cut first is the train trips, even if it means fewer chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother, who cleans offices, about your plans in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum cleans offices at night and she thinks an engineer is somebody who is set for life. I'd tell her the degree is fine but the debt is what scares me, and I'd ask her not to lend me the money she doesn't have. She'd lend it anyway, and that's why I don't tell her everything.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always about selling software and my degree keeps its value.
I'd tell my union group that **debt**, not AI, is what hurts graduates.
think: Privately I'm relieved my **degree** keeps its value.
Nothing fixes my **debt** or the few firms hiring near Dunmere, so I still worry about rent.
do: Finish the master's and keep the **supermarket shifts** three evenings a week.
Send about **30 applications** to firms within two hours by train.
feel: **Relieved** about the machines, tight in the chest about money.
S0.quote: I'd say good, because it means my degree keeps its value and the sums I'm learning are still the sums people need.
fieldNote: Sam's worry is **money**, not machines; the debt colours every answer here.
He is sure AI is **hype** and has never used it.
Interview trips cost him paid shifts, which is a concrete trade-off.

steps.text: Finish the structural engineering master's and keep three supermarket shifts a week
Send 30 applications to consultancies within two hours by train
Skip the cheaper conference trips and only travel for interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the bosses cashing in. If software does the checking and drafting, they'll hire fewer juniors and call it progress. I'd say it loudly in the student union, because someone has to make the point that regulation and union rules should come with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the entry jobs are exactly the thinking tasks: checking drawings, running loads, writing reports. I did that in my eight weeks at Kestrel Surveying. If the checking and drafting go to software, then there is no first rung for people like me, and I'm already competing for three or four graduate places nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay on and do a second year of study or a professional course to look more senior. I'd also push the student union to demand that employers take on trainees. I'd still refuse to use the chatbots, because I'd rather be slow and right, but I know that might cost me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and scared, mostly. Angry that people with money decide it and scared that I'm on the wrong side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a structural firm would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking drawings, writing the calculation reports, and booking site visits. Mr Hale, the senior engineer at Kestrel, did the signing off and the juniors did the rest. If the rest is automated, he doesn't need juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at a firm like Kestrel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other graduates, honestly, especially the ones who've never practised by hand. I'd worry about my friend Dara (a fellow student), who is brilliant but has no internship at all. If firms cut the entry places, she'll be the first one out.

say: I'd say employers will use software to **hire fewer juniors** and call it progress.
I'd push my union to demand **trainee places** and rules on AI.
think: The entry jobs are exactly the **checking and drafting** I did at Kestrel.
So the **first rung** may vanish, and only three or four graduate places exist nearby.
do: Look at a **professional course** to stay in study and look more senior.
Join the **student union** campaign for employer trainee quotas.
feel: **Angry** at employers and scared of being on the wrong side.
S1.quote: If the checking and drafting go to software, then there is no first rung for people like me, and I'm already competing for three or four graduate places nearby.
fieldNote: Sam names **employers** as the problem; his answer is collective, not personal.
He knows his internship tasks are the exposed ones, which is sharp insight.
Resistance to AI tools is a stance he admits could cost him.

steps.text: Join the student union campaign for trainee quotas at engineering firms
Enrol in a chartered engineer exam course after the master's
Write to the local councillor about public trainee schemes
Keep doing calculations by hand and checking them afterwards

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, the way you'd have after a flood. Somebody has to speak up for people at the start of their careers. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, because the companies certainly won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it ends my plans. I'd finish the master's in a world where nobody needs a graduate to do thinking work, and I'd have 31,000 of debt on top of it. I can't see a path, and the robots would come around 2031, so even the site work wouldn't be safe for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try to get any paid work I can, even site labouring or warehouse work, and stop the course if there's no point. I'd call the union and the student advice office about the debt. I don't have a real plan, and I'd be honest about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake doing sums that never add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do to the master's, which takes one more year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course has about eight months left, and dropping out wouldn't cancel the loan. So I'd be paying for a certificate nobody wants. I'd rather stop and work, but then I'd feel I'd thrown away two years of effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government if this were real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt relief first, then a guaranteed income while the economy sorts itself out, and a proper public jobs scheme. I'd want rules so firms that cut staff to buy machines pay into it. I'd vote for anyone who promised that.

say: I'd demand an **emergency plan** for people starting their careers, like after a flood.
I'd say firms that replace staff should **pay into** public support.
think: I think it **ends my plans** for a structural career.
I'd be left with **31,000 debt** and a certificate nobody wants.
do: Look for **any paid work**, including site labouring or warehouse shifts.
Ask the **student advice office** and the union what happens to my loan if I stop.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake doing sums that never add up.
S2.quote: I'd finish the master's in a world where nobody needs a graduate to do thinking work, and I'd have 31,000 of debt on top of it.
fieldNote: Two years is the one case where Sam has **no plan**, only a wish for public support.
He ties robots arriving in 2031 to site work, so the fallback is not safe either.
Sunk cost on the master's is a live dilemma.

steps.text: Ask the student advice office what happens to the loan if I stop
Apply for site labouring and warehouse jobs near Alder Row
Join union lobbying for debt relief and a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same fear but with a runway, and we should use that time to get rules in place. I'd go to the union meetings and tell people to write to their representatives now, not after it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I think there's still a way, but a narrow one. I'd finish the master's and get a job at a firm that does inspections or site supervision, where people still have to turn up. That's where the thinking AI is slower to reach. I'd rather be the person on the muddy site than the one at a screen, because that's where thinking AI is slower to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for site engineer and inspection roles first, and I'd pay down the debt as fast as I can while I'm still earning. Maybe 200 a month, not more. I'd also take a short course in site safety, which is hands-on and has a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier than before. Scared, but I can see some steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the last year I'd do a placement at a site rather than a desk, even if it paid nothing. I'd ask Mr Hale if Kestrel runs site teams. It's my best chance of a contact that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your last year of study look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives me nothing but panic. Five gives me a debt plan and a hands-on route, and that's a big difference for me. Ten gives me time to wait it out, but I'd still be watching the robots.

say: I'd tell people to **write to representatives** now while there is a runway.
I'd say the safest jobs are the ones where you must **turn up on site**.
think: Five years leaves a **narrow way** into site and inspection work.
That is where thinking AI is slower to reach, so there is a **debt plan** too.
do: Apply first to **site engineer and inspection** roles near Dunmere.
Pay **200 a month** off the debt once the first wage comes.
feel: **Steadier** than with two years: scared, but there are steps.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person on the muddy site than the one at a screen, because that's where thinking AI is slower to reach.
fieldNote: Time converts panic into a **hands-on plan**; Sam reads robots as slower than thinking AI.
He gets practical and specific: 200 a month, site safety licence.
Still avoids AI tools himself, even in the plan.

steps.text: Apply to site engineer and inspection roles near Dunmere
Put 200 a month towards the student loan from the first wage
Take a site safety licence course in the final term
Write to my representative about graduate trainee schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it out properly, with training funds and unions at the table. A decade is long enough to change rules if enough people push. I'd join the push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd probably be ahead of it. I'd have paid off most of the debt, built up a record on site and be about 34. I might be a senior engineer or a trainer of others by then. I'd still worry, but it's more like normal career worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the first graduate job anywhere, and save a bit each month. I'd get chartered by about 28 and look at moving into project management, which is people work. And I'd learn what these AI tools do, maybe, because ten years is long to ignore them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, to be honest. A bit sad that the world gets so jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about the course you chose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose structures where someone has to sign off and take legal responsibility. A machine can't be sued, and I think the law will keep a person in the chair that signs off structures. It's a guess, but it's the bet I'd make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big shareholders and the ministers who let it happen without a plan. Not the workers, and not the machines. I'd blame the people who could have slowed it and chose profit.

say: I'd say a decade is **long enough** to change the rules if enough people push.
I'd tell anyone starting out to get **chartered** early.
think: With ten years I'd probably be **ahead of it**, about 34 and well into my career.
Most of the **debt** would be paid and I'd have site experience.
do: Take the **first graduate job** anywhere and save each month.
Aim to get **chartered by 28** and move toward project management.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a little sadness that the world gets so jumpy.
S4.quote: A machine can't be sued, and I think the law will keep a person in the chair that signs off structures.
fieldNote: Sam's best case is the **long runway**; he finally considers tools he refused before.
His hope rests on the legal need for a signing engineer.
Blame goes to shareholders and ministers, which fits his progressive view.

steps.text: Take the first graduate engineering job offered, wherever it is
Save 150 a month once the debt payments are covered
Sit the chartered engineer exams by age 28
Try one AI drafting tool in a safe test project

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one worries me most, because it leaves no time and I'd have debt and no job. What would help is relief on the loan, a guaranteed income while things settle and a public scheme that places graduates in real work. I'd also need a union that actually bargains for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the machines themselves. I'm scared of who owns them and what they decide. If more people got a say, I'd be calmer.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machines themselves. I'm scared of who owns them and what they decide.
portrait: Sam is 24, doing a **structural engineering master's** after a civil engineering degree, with 31,000 of debt and no savings.
He works three evening shifts at a supermarket, and a short internship at a surveying firm showed him which tasks are exposed.
He is progressive, distrusts employers and **never uses AI**, preferring hand calculations.
His moods run from anxious to alarmed, worst with only two years, easing when a long runway gives him a plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most: no time, debt and no first job.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **loan relief**, a guaranteed income and a union that bargains for new graduates.
